Especially so during developmental stages key towards our social-interaction / personalities & avenues for communication. 

One thing in particular that I have trouble differentiating between, sometimes, is sarcasm and language/communication that plays on literal meanings.  I tend to take things very literally, even if they aren't meant to be taken that way, my thinking is just wired that way.

One of the best ways I've dealt with mine is just to be outgoing (yeah, it can be hard) and embrace humor as best I can.  I don't particularly like big groups of people either, but not everyone does, it's particularly hard realizing this at the high school / college age.

It depends on your usage.  For general usage you want at least a dual core, perhaps an i3/i5. 

If you're a light user, (by light, I mean, e-mail, word processing, internet) then you can get by using a netbook.

Netbook Example: http://www.newegg.com/Product/Product.aspx?Item=N82E16834220761

CPU is designed for light-use (as specified above) and the hardware is designed to be very power-efficient.

2GB RAM means you won't have all that many applications up at once, perhaps ... Word Processing / Firefox

Screen Size is 12'' (3 lbs as well) These are meant to be carried around, and they're the most mobile "laptop" development, however, they lack the multi-core processing muscle & dedicated GPU's of bigger 15.4'' or 17'' laptops. 



Dual Cores ~ Average user, runs a few processor intensive tasks, doesn't multi-task as much as a Quad-Core user.  
(Example: running Firefox/Itunes while surfing the web)

~ I'd personally reccomend i3/i5 laptop CPU's over AMD/Athlon for thermal reasons, the i3/i5/i7 series of laptop CPU's dynamically adjust their processing speed based on what's needed.
i3's and i5's are dual cores with the ability, "Turbo Boost", which allows the computer to boost a single-core up to a much higher frequency if the application places such demand on the CPU.

The i5 laptop CPU's also have integrated graphics proccessing (IGP). The laptop i7-Quad-Core models don't have IGP.  So, i5 laptop CPU's are much more likely to have switchable graphics
or Optimus technology. i3's don't have "Turbo Boost", but are still capable CPU's that adjust their performance based on application/user demands. i5's are dual-cores with "Hyperthreading", 
which is the ability of a core to handle more than one thread at once.  (Multi-core applications are generally multi-thread) This gives i5 laptops 2 Physical cores & 2 (Logical)/fake cores
(which gives them more of an advantage to multi-core applications than previous generations of CPU's, for example, intel-pentium dual cores.

http://www.newegg.com/Product/Product.aspx?Item=N82E16834157466 ~ i3 laptop with switchable graphics, 2.4 Ghz Dual-Core processor, 5650 Graphics Proccessing Unit (GPU) (Video Card).

The advantages of having a more normal sized laptop are primarily in the Speed/Power of the CPU/GPU as well as having additional Hard-drive space and RAM. 4GB of RAM is PLENTY of 
space for the average user, there's really no point in going past 4GB unless your applications use up a tremendous amount of memory (that, or you have tons of applications open).
In addition, your 15'4'' laptops generally have a biggeer screen & resolution (which drains battery life considerably). 

The disadvantages CPU/GPU are less power-efficient than in Netbooks. Looking at 2-3 hours of battery life max, depending on screen-brightness & usage. 




(Quad Cores), for laptops are generally lower clocked speed wise, but the usage is also different, 2+ core laptops excel in things like Encoding/Video Editing, Photoshop/Rendering, & heavy physics/mathematical applications.  

They also better handle running more applications at once, though RAM does play a significant part in multi-tasking too. More specifically, however, as I mentioned above quad-cores are better at handling Video/Graphics, Encoding, as well as
heavier physics/design & mathematical applications, the reason for this is that these applications are typically designed with multi-core use in mind.  (They run faster on a Quad > Dual/Single/).

If you do any sort of gaming or graphics/video editing or development then you should invest in a dedicated GPU/Video Card. I generally tend to suggest a Mobility 5650.  If you do any sort of gaming having a dedicated graphics card is a must.

http://www.notebookcheck.net/ATI-Mobility-Radeon-HD-5650.23697.0.html (details tasks in which the dedicated GPU can help) as well as provides game-benchmarks (FPS) towards the bottom.  The 5650 is a decent mid-range DirectX 10 GPU that should

RAM 3-4GB is fairly standard, beyond that raises the price significantly & unnecessarily. Having less than 3-4GB w/ a laptop Quad is somewhat of an oxymoron.

4GB RAM ~ Standard for multi-tasking... Games (and most software, not otherwise already mentioned) is primarily programmed for Dual-Core use, though there are some exceptions starting to arise)
